true_positives.golden_comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reminder cancellation is now fire-and-forget although the DB write is the only cancellation mechanism

`deleteScheduledEmailReminder` and `deleteScheduledSMSReminder` are async and are called inside `forEach` without being awaited. Previously the reminder DB deletions were collected and awaited in `Promise.all`. Now the DB update (`cancelled: true`) or delete is the only thing that stops the email, and nothing waits for it. In a serverless environment the work can be dropped once the response is sent, which silently reintroduces the 'reminder still sent for a cancelled booking' bug. The same pattern appears in bookings.tsx (requestReschedule), handleNewBooking.ts and several places in workflows.tsx. Collect the promises and await them (e.g. add them to the `Promise.all`).

true_positives.golden_comment: When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`immediateDelete` path still uses the limited SendGrid cancel API, with no DB flag and no fallback

The PR exists because SendGrid allows at most 100 pending cancellations. Yet `immediateDelete` still POSTs `status: cancel` straight to SendGrid. It is used for rescheduled bookings (handleNewBooking), deleted workflows and deleted steps. Reschedules and large workflow deletions can therefore still hit the 100-cancel cap. When the call fails, the error is only logged and the reminder is neither marked `cancelled` nor deleted. The email is then sent anyway, which is the original bug. On success the row is also left untouched (not flagged, not deleted), so a later cancel or reschedule of the same booking sends a duplicate cancel for the same batch. For the reschedule case the booking and its reminders are retained, so simply setting `cancelled: true` (the deferred path) would avoid the limit. At minimum, fall back to `cancelled: true` when the immediate cancel fails.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.

false_positives.candidate:
Cancellations made shortly before send time can be missed by the 15-minute cron

A cancelled reminder is only handed to SendGrid when the cron runs within the hour before `scheduledDate`. The cron runs every 15 minutes, and a cancellation made after the last run before the send time is never processed. The first-step `deleteMany` then removes the row after the send time, and the email goes out for a cancelled or rescheduled booking. Likewise, any skipped or failed cron run in that window loses the cancellation. This is an inherent limitation of the deferred design and should at least be documented. A mitigation would be to cancel directly when the reminder is within the last 15 minutes, or to widen the window.

Cron cancel loop aborts on first SendGrid error and defers all DB deletes until the end

All SendGrid cancel calls and the `workflowReminder.delete` queries sit inside one try/catch. The delete queries are only awaited via `Promise.all` after the loop finishes. If any `client.request` throws (batch already sent, already cancelled, 4xx or 5xx), the catch swallows it. The remaining reminders are never cancelled, so those emails go out. The reminders already cancelled at SendGrid are never deleted from the DB because `Promise.all` is not reached. On the next run they are re-sent to SendGrid. If SendGrid rejects a cancel for an already-cancelled batch, the same failing reminder aborts the loop again and again. One bad record can therefore block every later cancellation until its `scheduledDate` passes. Handle each reminder in its own try/catch and delete (or flag) each row right after its successful cancel.

No tests for the new cancel flow or cron cancellation step

The PR changes the cancellation contract of `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` and `deleteScheduledSMSReminder` (new signature, new `cancelled` column, new deferred cron step). It adds no tests for the deferred flag, the immediate path, the null-`referenceId` path, or the cron picking up `cancelled` reminders within the one-hour window. The previous fix (#6991) failed silently for the same lack of coverage.

Reschedule re-cancels reminders already cancelled by requestReschedule and ignores the `cancelled` flag

When an organizer uses `requestReschedule`, the old booking's email reminders are only flagged `cancelled: true`. The attendee then books a new slot via handleNewBooking, which loads `originalRescheduledBooking.workflowReminders`, including the already-flagged ones. For each of them it calls `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(..., true)` and sends a second SendGrid cancel for the same batch. That wastes pending-cancel slots and may error. Because the call is not awaited and errors are only logged, a failure leaves things unflagged. The loop should skip reminders where `cancelled` is already true. It should also prefer the deferred path (flag only) over the immediate SendGrid cancel.

Unused `Prisma` import and type-only symbols turned into value imports

After removing `PrismaPromise<Prisma.BatchPayload>[]`, `Prisma` is no longer referenced anywhere in this file but was added as a value import. `PrismaPromise` was also changed from `import type` to a regular value import although it is only used as a type. This produces an unused-import lint error. The same unnecessary `import type` to value-import change was made for `App`, `Credential`, `EventTypeCustomInput` and `Prisma` in handleNewBooking.ts. Restore the `import type` form.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
async forEach callback makes the surrounding try/catch ineffective and leaves deletions un-awaited

The callback is now `async` and awaits `getCalendar`. `forEach` ignores the returned promises, so the enclosing `try/catch` can no longer catch anything from `getCalendar` or `deleteEvent`. A failure, such as a CalendarService constructor throwing (which the old synchronous code would have caught and logged), becomes an unhandled promise rejection. The function also proceeds to send the reschedule email and `return true` before the calendar/video deletions have run. In a serverless handler the work can be cut off. Use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(...))` (or a `for...of` loop with await) inside the try.

true_positives.golden_comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully

The callback is now `async` and awaits `getCalendar`. `forEach` ignores the returned promises, so the enclosing `try/catch` can no longer catch anything from `getCalendar` or `deleteEvent`. A failure, such as a CalendarService constructor throwing (which the old synchronous code would have caught and logged), becomes an unhandled promise rejection. The function also proceeds to send the reschedule email and `return true` before the calendar/video deletions have run. In a serverless handler the work can be cut off. Use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(...))` (or a `for...of` loop with await) inside the try.

false_positives.candidate:
Recurring-cancel branch still uses async forEach, so deletions are neither awaited nor tracked in apiDeletes

The PR converted the sibling legacy branch (lines ~477-483) from `forEach` to `for...of` with `await getCalendar`, so its promises land in `apiDeletes` before `Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` runs. The recurring branch keeps `forEach(async ...)`. There, `apiDeletes.push(deletedEvent)` happens only after `await getCalendar(...)` and `await calendar.deleteEvent(...)`. By then `Promise.all` has already snapshotted `apiDeletes`, and the handler may have returned. The calendar events for the remaining recurring bookings are therefore not awaited and their errors are unhandled. Use a `for...of` loop (or `Promise.all` over `map`) so these deletions are actually part of `apiDeletes`. The `calendar` fetched at line 452 is also unused in this branch.

async forEach callback makes the surrounding try/catch ineffective and leaves deletions un-awaited

Same issue as in the vital app. `forEach(async ...)` with `await getCalendar(...)` means errors from `getCalendar`/`deleteEvent` bypass the `try/catch` and become unhandled rejections. The calendar and video deletions are not awaited before the email is sent and `true` is returned. Previously a synchronous throw from `getCalendar` would have been caught and logged. Replace with `await Promise.all(refs.map(...))` or a `for...of` loop.

import() calls in the object literal run eagerly, so nothing is lazy-loaded

Every entry is `import("./x")`, and a dynamic import starts as soon as it is evaluated. All ~29 app modules therefore load when `@calcom/app-store` is first imported, so the cost is the same as the old static `import * as` and the lazy-loading benefit is lost. It also adds a failure mode: each promise is created up front and nobody awaits the ones that aren't used. If any single app module fails to import (missing optional dependency, bad env access at module scope), that promise rejects with no handler. That raises an unhandledRejection at startup (a process crash on Node 15+ defaults) even for code paths that never touch that app. The entries should be thunks, e.g. `applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")`, awaited per call site, so only the needed app loads and errors surface where it is used.

requestReschedule fires un-awaited async deletions with no error handling

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async ...)` now awaits `getCalendar` inside a fire-and-forget callback. Nothing awaits the calendar or video deletions, and any rejection from `getCalendar` or `deleteEvent` is an unhandled rejection that nothing logs. The mutation continues to send emails and webhooks and resolves before the previous calendar/video events are removed. In a serverless runtime the pending work may never finish. Collect the promises and `await Promise.all(...)` (with per-item error handling) before continuing.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`end` is computed from slotStartTime, so the slot end is never checked against working hours

`const end = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();` is identical to `start`. The intent was clearly the slot end (`slotEndTime`). As written, `end > workingHour.endTime` is just a check on the start time, so a slot that starts inside working hours but runs past their end passes. The check is effectively broken.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Object identity comparison with `===` on dayjs objects is always false

`dayjs(date.start).add(...) === dayjs(date.end).add(...)` compares two freshly created objects by reference, so it never evaluates to true. This branch was meant to handle a zero-length override (the day marked unavailable). It is dead code, so that case relies on the later `isBefore`/`isAfter` checks. Compare with `.isSame()` or `.valueOf()`.

false_positives.candidate:
Multiple date-override ranges on the same day make every slot unavailable

The `dateOverrides.find` callback returns true (slot unavailable) as soon as the slot is outside any single override on that date. A host with two override ranges on one day (for example 09:00–12:00 and 14:00–17:00) has each valid slot fail the other range's checks. A 10:00 slot is before the 14:00 range and so returns true, and the function returns false. The slot has to be rejected only if it fits none of the overrides for that date. Cal.com's date-override UI allows multiple ranges per date, so this makes valid slots disappear for those hosts.

No test for the headline fix (fixed-host date overrides in round-robin)

The PR's main fix is that fixed hosts' date overrides and working hours are enforced in `checkIfIsAvailable` for round-robin events. The only new test is a personal-event invitee-timezone case. Nothing covers a ROUND_ROBIN event with a fixed host having an override, multiple overrides on one day, split working hours, or an override spanning UTC midnight. Those are the cases where the bugs above show up. Also, `toHaveTimeSlots` only iterates the actual slots, so a result with fewer slots than expected still passes.

Offset derived from `Date.toString()` and possibly undefined timeZone

`dayjs(override.start.toString())` re-parses a host-locale string such as 'Tue Jul 04 2023 14:00:00 GMT+0000 (...)'. That is implementation-dependent and drops milliseconds; pass `override.start` directly. `override.timeZone` is optional in the updated `TimeRange` type. When it is missing, `.tz(undefined)` silently falls back to the runtime's local timezone, giving a different offset on client and server.

Override matched by UTC calendar date of its start only; overrides crossing UTC midnight are skipped

After shifting the override start to real UTC, the code matches an override to a slot only if the UTC date of the override start equals the UTC date of the slot start. An override that spans UTC midnight is common for hosts far from UTC, for example 06:00–12:00 in Sydney, which runs from 20:00Z the previous day to 02:00Z. Slots on the later UTC date never match, so `dateOverrideExist` stays false. Those slots fall through to the regular working-hours check and the override is ignored for them. The comparison should use the organizer-local date, or check whether the slot falls inside the [start, end) instant range.

Override-to-day filter is not timezone-adjusted, but the time conversion now is

`activeOverrides` still selects overrides whose raw `start` (the organizer's wall-clock time encoded as UTC) falls between the invitee's start and end of day. The new code then shifts the minutes by the invitee-vs-organizer offset. The day selection and the time conversion therefore use different frames. For an invitee far ahead of the organizer (for example UTC+10 and an organizer in IST), the override's real instant is on invitee day D, but the raw start falls on D+1. The override is dropped from day D and applied to D+1 at the shifted time. The filter should run on the converted start, using the same offset.

Shifted override minutes wrap at midnight, producing inverted or wrongly-placed ranges

Start and end are converted to `hour()*60 + minute()` after adding the offset, which discards the day. If the shift pushes an override across the invitee's midnight, start and end wrap to small values. A late-evening override such as 18:00–23:59 in the organizer's timezone, viewed from a timezone further east, can give an end value smaller than the start, which `buildSlots` skips (`start >= end`), so the slots vanish. If only one side wraps, the range is placed on the wrong day. Clamp or split the range at the invitee's day boundaries instead of taking time-of-day modulo 24h.

Working-hours check rejects any slot that falls outside any one range for that day

`workingHours.find(cb)` returns true, and the slot is rejected, as soon as the slot lies outside any single working-hour entry whose `days` includes the slot's weekday. A user with split availability on the same days (for example 09:00–12:00 and 13:00–17:00, or a lunch break) has two entries for those days. A slot inside the first range is always outside the second, so `find` matches and `checkIfIsAvailable` returns false. Every slot for such a host is then dropped. The check should pass if the slot lies inside at least one range (`!workingHours.some(contains slot)`), and it should apply only when entries exist for that day. Because `...schedule` is spread into every fixed and loose host check, this regresses ordinary non-round-robin events too.

true_positives.golden_comment: OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OAuth `state` is a deterministic pipeline signature, not a per-session nonce

The `state` sent to GitHub and later compared (line 412) is `pipeline.signature`. It is derived from the pipeline's views and is the same for every user and org; the tests reuse the same hard-coded value for two different orgs and users. It is therefore guessable and gives no CSRF or session binding for the OAuth authorize round trip. Anyone can craft a callback URL with their own `code` and the known `state`. The comparison is also a plain `!=` rather than a constant-time compare. For a security fix whose description lists the state check as a protection, use a random, session-bound value.

KeyError/500 when existing Integration has no `sender` metadata

For such an Integration that has no OrganizationIntegration (for example, a re-install after the org integration was removed), the lookup raises KeyError and the user gets a 500 instead of the friendly error page. Authorize URL query string is built by string interpolation without encoding

`client_id`, `state` and `redirect_uri` are interpolated directly into the authorize URL. `redirect_uri` is a full URL containing `:` and `/`, and it is not percent-encoded. It works with GitHub today, but it is fragile, for example with a customized `url-prefix`, and `urlencode` should be used.

The PR lists three failure causes: user mismatch, state mismatch, and a failed `code` exchange. Only the user mismatch is tested. Nothing covers a wrong `state`, an `access_token` exchange failure, a `/user` response with no `login`, or an Integration that exists with no `sender` metadata. There is also no positive test where the authenticated GitHub user matches `metadata["sender"]["login"]` for a pre-existing Integration. Without these, the new validation can regress, or crash as in the KeyError case, unnoticed.

test_installation_not_found no longer tests the installation-not-found path

The test still stubs the installation lookup with a 404. The `IntegrationError("The GitHub installation could not be found.")` branch in `build_integration` is therefore no longer covered, and the old assertion was silently replaced. true_positives.matched_candidate:
Inconsistent metric tag names (`shard` vs `shards`) for the same shard_tag

`spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` are tagged with `shard`, while `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` uses `shards`. Both carry the same comma-joined value. Dashboards that group or filter by tag will miss one of the two. Pick one name. Also note that the comma-joined list becomes a tag value whose cardinality depends on the shard-to-process assignment.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
time.sleep(0.1) added to fix a race is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched

`test_basic` begins with `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)`. The newly added `time.sleep(0.1)`, commented "Give flusher threads time to process after drift change", calls that patched function and does nothing. The flusher thread therefore still races with `step.join()`, which sets `stopped` right after the drift change, so `(msg,) = messages` can fail intermittently. Wait explicitly instead, for example by polling until `messages` is non-empty with a deadline, or capture the real `time.sleep` before patching.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) is False for SpawnProcess, so hung flushers are never killed

The flusher processes come from `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process`, which is `SpawnProcess`. `SpawnProcess` derives from `BaseProcess`, not from `multiprocessing.context.Process`, which is what `multiprocessing.Process` names. The `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` guard is therefore always False for real processes, and `process.kill()` is never called. The old code called `self.process.kill()` unconditionally. In the `cause == "hang"` case the old process is left running and `_create_process_for_shards` starts a second flusher for the same shards. Two flushers then compete over the same Redis keys, which can cause duplicate or fragmented segments and leaked processes. Fix this by checking `hasattr(process, 'kill')`, by checking `not isinstance(process, threading.Thread)`, or by using `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess`. The same wrong check in `join()` means `terminate()` is also never called.

true_positives.golden_comment: Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
time.sleep(0.1) added to fix a race is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched

`test_basic` begins with `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)`. The newly added `time.sleep(0.1)`, commented "Give flusher threads time to process after drift change", calls that patched function and does nothing. The flusher thread therefore still races with `step.join()`, which sets `stopped` right after the drift change, so `(msg,) = messages` can fail intermittently. Wait explicitly instead, for example by polling until `messages` is non-empty with a deadline, or capture the real `time.sleep` before patching.

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
join() breaks out of the loop on deadline without terminating remaining processes

When the deadline expires, `join()` does `break`, so the `process.terminate()` call at the bottom of the loop never runs for the remaining processes. They are only reaped as daemons at interpreter exit. Terminating should happen for every process even if the wait budget is exhausted, and the unused `process_index` loop variable can be dropped.

false_positives.candidate:
Docstring says one process per shard, but shards are capped and shared

The class docstring says "Creates one process per shard". That is wrong, because `max_processes` caps the process count and shards are distributed round-robin across processes, so one process can serve several shards. The CLI default `--flusher-processes=1` runs a single process for all shards. The `:param topic:` entry is also stale, since no such parameter exists, and `max_processes` is undocumented.

Memory check queries Redis once per flusher buffer on every submit

The memory-pressure check in `submit()` used to call `get_memory_info()` on a single buffer. It now calls it on every per-process buffer in `self.buffers`. Assuming `get_memory_info()` reports on the whole Redis cluster rather than only the buffer's assigned shards (not checked here), each call repeats the same `INFO` queries. `submit()` then does up to N times more Redis round trips per batch, and the used/available sums are inflated N-fold, which cancels out in the ratio. Query one buffer, or deduplicate by node, instead.

New test only checks process bookkeeping, not multi-process flushing or restarts

`test_flusher_processes_limit` checks only the process count and the shard-to-process map. It never submits spans on multiple shards and checks that segments are flushed, and it never covers the restart, hang or crash paths in `_ensure_processes_alive`, nor the per-process backpressure aggregation. The restart path is where the `isinstance`/`kill` regression lives, and nothing exercises it.

No validation of max_processes; negative values crash with KeyError

`max_processes or len(assigned_shards)` treats 0 as "one per shard", but a negative value from `--flusher-processes -1` (click `type=int` accepts it) is kept. `num_processes = min(-1, n)` is -1, so `process_to_shards_map` is empty and `i % self.num_processes` yields an index that is not in the map, which raises a KeyError at consumer startup. Validate `>= 1`, for example with `click.IntRange(min=1)` on the option.

Unused helper _create_process_for_shard

`_create_process_for_shard(self, shard)` is never called; the restart path uses `_create_process_for_shards` directly. It is dead code that adds API surface and a second way to restart processes.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Error-handling test asserts the opposite of its stated intent and is timing dependent

`test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling` is documented as "errors in processing don't block offset commits". The worker's `finally` completes the offset even when the processor raises, so both offsets 100 and 101 become committable at the next 1s commit tick. The assertion `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets` requires that nothing was committed. It passes only if the test finishes before the commit thread's next tick, and fails if the loop straddles a tick. It therefore does not verify the documented behaviour and can flake. It should wait for the commit and assert that offset 102 (the next offset to read) is committed.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.

false_positives.candidate:
"Graceful" shutdown discards items still queued

`shutdown()` sets `worker.shutdown = True` before calling `q.shutdown(immediate=False)`. The worker loop checks `self.shutdown` at the top of each iteration, so each worker finishes only its current item and exits, leaving the rest of its queue unprocessed. `close()` also joins the commit thread before shutting down the pool, so work finished during shutdown is never committed. This does not lose offsets, because they simply stay uncommitted, but it contradicts the docstring and causes avoidable reprocessing. Either drain the queues (let `queue.ShutDown` end the workers) or fix the docstring.

Any exception in submit() marks the offset completed, so failed enqueues are silently dropped and committed

The `except Exception` branch in `submit` calls `add_offset` and `complete_offset` for the message, which makes it immediately committable. That is fine for an undecodable payload. It is data loss when the failure is in `queue_pool.submit`, for example `queue.ShutDown` from a shut-down queue, or an error in `grouping_fn`. The message is never processed, its offset is committed past, and the only trace is a log line. Infrastructure failures should propagate, or the offset should not be completed, so the message is retried after a restart.

Commit logic treats any gap in offsets as unprocessed and stalls commits permanently

`get_committable_offsets` walks `range(start, max_offset + 1)` and stops at the first offset that is not in `all_offsets`. Kafka partitions can legitimately have non-contiguous offsets (transaction markers, compacted topics, retention). The tracker only knows offsets it was given, so it cannot tell "never delivered" from "in flight". After such a gap, `highest_committable` never advances. Commits stop for that partition, and `all_offsets` and `outstanding` grow without bound. The tests (`test_offset_gaps_block_commits`, `test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_gaps`) enshrine this behaviour. Commit decisions should rely on the lowest outstanding offset (commit everything below it), not on contiguity of submitted offsets.

Kafka commit is invoked from a background thread while the main thread polls

`_commit_loop` runs in its own daemon thread and calls `commit_function`, which wraps the arroyo `commit` callable. That callable is wired to the `StreamProcessor` and its Kafka consumer, which stages and commits offsets and are not thread-safe. They are normally used only from the processor's run loop, the same thread that polls and handles assignment and revocation callbacks. Calling them concurrently from the commit thread risks racing with `poll`, assignment and revocation state, and committing partitions that were just revoked. The strategy should hand the committable offsets back to the main thread (for example, compute them in `poll()` and call `commit` there) instead of committing from a separate thread.

Probabilistic assertions in queue tests can flake

`test_stats_reporting` asserts `stats["total_items"] > 0` immediately after submitting, but three live workers may already have drained all 10 trivial items. `test_different_groups_distributed` (line 106) asserts that 20 string keys hit all 3 queues. Python's string hash is randomized per process, so there is a small chance (about 0.1%) that some queue is missed. Both tests should use deterministic setup, such as blocking the workers or choosing keys by computed queue index.

Queues are unbounded and poll() applies no backpressure, contrary to the class docstring

The strategy docstring promises "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but each queue is `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize`, and `poll()` only emits a gauge. `submit` never raises `MessageRejected`, so the consumer keeps pulling from Kafka at full speed. If one queue is slow or stuck, committed offsets stall at the first outstanding offset, which is exactly the case the PR describes. Meanwhile every later message is decoded and held in memory, each with both the decoded result and the original message in `WorkItem`. A stuck worker therefore leads to unbounded memory growth and a large reprocessing burst on restart. Use bounded queues and reject or pause submission when the target queue is full.

Strategy close() shuts down the factory-shared queue pool, which is reused after the first rebalance

`FixedQueuePool` is created once in `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` and passed to every `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` that `create_with_partitions` builds. Arroyo calls `close()`/`join()` on the current strategy on every partition revocation and then calls `create_with_partitions` again. `close()` and `join()` both call `queue_pool.shutdown()`, which sets `worker.shutdown = True`, calls `q.shutdown()` on every queue and joins the workers. After the first rebalance the replacement strategy is handed the same dead pool: the worker threads have exited and `queue.put` raises `ShutDown`. Combined with the broad `except` in `submit`, every later message is dropped and its offset is committed (see the next finding). The `OffsetTracker` is also shared across rebalances, so leftover offsets for revoked partitions can be committed later and rewind the group's progress. The pool needs to be owned by the factory and only shut down in `factory.shutdown()`, or be created per strategy instance, and the tracker should be reset for revoked partitions.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Underscore-joined denial key is ambiguous and can deny the wrong resource

The key joins userUID, action, name and parent with `_`, and these values can contain underscores. `(name="a_b", parent="c")` and `(name="a", parent="b_c")` both produce `..._a_b_c`. A cached denial for one resource then wrongly denies the other for up to 30s. The key also starts with the same `perm_<uid>_<action>` prefix as `userPermCacheKey`, which makes cross-key clashes possible if values contain underscores. Use an unambiguous separator or encoding, or a distinct prefix such as `perm_denied_`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache key omits identity type, so renderer and anonymous share denials

`userPermDenialCacheKey` is built from `checkReq.UserUID` (the raw subject ID), not the identity type. `anonymous:0` and `render:0` both yield UserUID `0` (the tests use exactly these subjects). If an anonymous check on dashboard X is denied, the key `<ns>.perm_0_dashboards:read_X_<folder>` is stored. A `render:0` check on the same dashboard within 30s then hits that entry in `Check` and is denied. The renderer holds a wildcard read grant, so image rendering can fail spuriously. Include the identity type in the key.

Denial entries are never invalidated and can mask a permission granted shortly after

A denial is cached for 30s with no invalidation. It is checked before the cached permissions and before the DB requery. If a check for a resource runs before its permission rows exist, or before a grant takes effect, the user is denied for the full TTL even though the DB now allows it. For example, a check may run between resource creation and permission assignment. That is the same "cannot fetch what I just created" symptom the PR targets. Consider a much shorter TTL for denials, or invalidation on resource creation or permission change.

Every non-allowed check not already in the denial cache hits the permission DB

Cached permissions that do not allow the request now fall through to `getIdentityPermissions`. `getUserPermissions` no longer consults `permCache`, so it always runs the permission query, and the denial cache is keyed per (name, folder). A user or client probing many distinct resources the user cannot access triggers one full permission query per resource. Singleflight only dedups concurrent calls for the same user and action. The first denied check for each resource therefore costs a DB round trip, which amplifies load. Consider rate-limiting the refetch, for example a short per-user/action refresh cooldown, instead of re-querying on every miss.

Requery path still uses a stale cached folder tree, then caches the resulting denial

After a cache miss, permissions are re-fetched from the DB, but `checkPermission` → `checkInheritedPermissions` → `buildFolderTree` still reads the folder tree from `folderCache` (30s TTL). Suppose a user with inherited access via parent folder P creates subfolder C and a dashboard in C. If the cached tree predates C, `tree.Ancestors(C)` is empty, so the check returns denied. This PR then writes a 30s denial entry for it. The newly created nested folder or dashboard stays inaccessible for up to 30s, which is the scenario the PR is meant to fix. The folder tree should be refreshed on the requery path, or denials caused by a possibly stale tree should not be cached.

Tests do not cover writing the denial entry, and a dead cacheHit branch remains

`TestService_CacheCheck` only checks that a pre-seeded denial entry is honored. No test verifies that a real denied `Check` writes `permDenialCache`, that a repeated denied check skips the DB (via `store.calls`), or that anonymous and renderer identities are handled. List fallback to the DB on a cache miss is untested. Separately, removing the "cached" case from `TestService_getUserPermissions` leaves the `cacheHit` field and its assertions as dead code, because no case sets `cacheHit: true`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing `key` on GrafanaRuleListItem in the filtered rules list

The previous `GrafanaRuleLoader` element had `key={key}`. The new `<GrafanaRuleListItem ... />` returned from `rules.map` has no key. The other `datasource` and `default` branches still pass `key`. React will warn about missing keys. Reconciliation falls back to index, so as filtered results stream in or get reordered, rows can reuse the wrong component state. That includes each row's delete modal, silence drawer and clone-redirect state, because `RuleActionsButtons` holds `useState`. Pass `key={key}` as before.

true_positives.golden_comment: RuleActionsButtons is invoked with only promRule, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer inside RuleActionsButtons still depends on a Grafana Ruler rule being present, so for Grafana rules coming from list views the 'Silence notifications' menu entry (now driven by Grafana Prom abilities) will toggle showSilenceDrawer without ever rendering the drawer. This means clicking 'Silence notifications' for these rules has no visible effect, even when abilities indicate silencing is allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Silence menu item is shown but the drawer never opens in the list view

`AlertRuleMenu` shows 'Silence notifications' from the prom-rule ability and calls `handleSilence`, which sets `showSilenceDrawer` to true. The drawer is only rendered when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) && showSilenceDrawer`. In the list view `rule` (the ruler rule) is undefined, so the condition is always false. Clicking Silence does nothing, which is a dead menu entry. The drawer needs to be driven by the prom rule, or the item hidden when no ruler rule is available.

false_positives.candidate:
Delete and Pause menu items can never render in the list view (no rulerRule)

The list view now passes only `promRule`, and `rulerRule` is undefined. `canDelete`/`canPause` are computed from the prom-rule abilities, but the items are still gated on a ruler rule. Delete is wrapped in `canDelete && rulerRule`, and Pause requires `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)`. So in the Grafana alert list, Delete and Pause are silently dropped even for users with permission. `showDivider` still counts `canPause`, so a stray divider can appear. The new `GrafanaGroupLoader` test also encodes this: delete permission is granted, yet it asserts exactly 4 menu items with no Delete. The Delete handler and `MenuItemPauseRule` need to work from the prom rule or a rule identifier, not `RulerRuleDTO`.

Export/Pause/Restore/DeletePermanently disabled for Grafana recording rules in the new prom hook

The ruler-based hook gates ModifyExport, Pause, Restore and DeletePermanently on `isGrafanaManagedAlertRule`, which is true for both alerting and recording Grafana rules. The new `useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities` gates them on `isAlertingRule` (`prometheusRuleType.grafana.alertingRule`). The in-code comment says 'All GrafanaPromRuleDTO rules are Grafana-managed by definition', which contradicts this. Result: recording rules lose Export and Pause in the list view, which they previously had. Only Silence should be restricted to alerting rules. The new tests use only alerting rules, so this is not covered.

Federated rule group check dropped for the deprecated useAllAlertRuleAbilities path

`useAllAlertRuleAbilities` used to compute `isFederated = isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)`, which made federated (Mimir `source_tenants`) groups immutable. It now delegates to `useAllRulerRuleAbilities`, which hardcodes `isFederated = false` with a TODO. Every existing caller (e.g. `RulesTable`, `RuleDetails`) therefore now offers Edit, Delete and Pause on federated rule groups. This is a silent behaviour regression unrelated to the stated goal of removing the ruler from the list view. Pass the federated flag through, or keep the old check in the deprecated wrapper.

GrafanaGroupLoader docs still say it loads from the Ruler endpoint

The component doc ('Loads an evaluation group from Prometheus and Ruler endpoints') and the `expectedRulesCount` comment ('Ruler response might contain different number of rules') are now wrong. The ruler query was removed and the component only uses the Prometheus endpoint.

Stale comment and variable name referring to ruler preload

The ruler prefetch dispatch was removed, but the comment ('This is not mandatory to preload ruler rules...') and the variable `cacheAndRulerPreload` still describe ruler preloading. This misleads readers into thinking ruler data is still loaded here. Rename and update the comment.

Tests lose coverage of removed behaviours and lock in the missing Delete/Pause actions

The tests for creating/deleting operation states and for `matchRules` were removed. The one remaining menu test grants delete and update permissions but asserts exactly four items (silence, copy link, duplicate, export), so it passes even though Delete and Pause are missing. There is no test that clicking Silence opens the drawer, or that Delete or Pause work from the list view. The RulesTable negative tests pass trivially because the default mocks return `[false, false]` for every ability.

returnTo parameter dropped from rule view link

The removed `GrafanaRuleLoader`/`GrafanaRuleListItem` built the href with `createRelativeUrl(..., { returnTo: createReturnTo() })`. The new component links to `/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view` with no `returnTo`. The rule view page can therefore no longer send the user back to the filtered list or position they came from. Nothing in the PR says this was intended, and the updated tests only check `stringContaining('/alerting/grafana/<uid>/view')`, so they would not catch it.

true_positives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New interpolation tests do not cover scopedVars or ad-hoc filter forwarding

The new 'Interpolates queries before execution' tests only exercise the mocked `replace` on `$__auto` and `$step`. Nothing verifies that `request.scopedVars` and `request.filters` are forwarded to `applyTemplateVariables`, which is the new contract in both runSplitQuery and runShardSplitQuery. Nothing verifies that ad-hoc filters end up in the executed sub-queries. There is also no test that the interpolated step is what feeds `calculateStep` for grouping, which is the point of the fix. A regression that drops the filters argument would pass these tests.

false_positives.candidate:
Empty-expression filter runs before interpolation

Targets are filtered with `.filter((query) => query.expr)` before `applyTemplateVariables`. A query whose expression is only a variable that resolves to an empty string, such as `$myQuery`, therefore survives as an empty expr after interpolation. It then flows into `isLogsQuery`, `querySupportsSplitting`, `calculateStep` and the request, instead of being dropped as an empty query. The same ordering is used in shardQuerySplitting.ts (hide and expr filters before the map). The old shard code filtered after interpolation, so this is a behaviour change there. Run the empty-expression filter after the interpolation map.

Shard path now interpolates the same queries repeatedly (once up front, again per sub-request)

runShardSplitQuery now calls applyTemplateVariables on every target. Each shard-group sub-request is then passed to runSplitQuery, which this PR also changed to call applyTemplateVariables on every target. DataSourceWithBackend.query() interpolates once more when runQuery executes. So each query is interpolated 1 + N + N times, where N is the number of shard groups and time chunks. Each pass re-runs addAdHocFilters, which does a Loki AST parse and rewrite. Ad-hoc filters are re-applied to already-filtered expressions, and text that is already interpolated is run through the template engine again. The result is wasted CPU on every sub-request, plus a risk of re-substituting `$…` text that was produced by a first-pass variable value. Interpolate once at the top-level entry point, or have the shard path tell runSplitQuery to skip re-interpolation.

Test hard-codes the redundant interpolation count (5 calls)

The assertion changed from `interpolateVariablesInQueries` being called once to `applyTemplateVariables` being called 5 times. That is 1 call from runShardSplitQuery plus 4 from runSplitQuery, one per sub-request. The test pins the double interpolation as expected behaviour. It will break whenever the number of shards or groups changes, and it will fail if the redundancy is later fixed. It should assert that interpolation happened and that the final queries are correct, not the exact call count.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `TestLogger.FromContext` method returns a new `TestLogger` instance via `NewTestLogger()` instead of returning the receiver (f). This causes logs to be recorded on an un-referenced instance, leading to broken test assertions that expect logs to be recorded on the original logger.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TestLogger.FromContext returns a fresh logger and discards recorded calls

`TestLogger.FromContext` returns `NewTestLogger()`, a new instance that does not share state with the receiver. LoggerMiddleware now calls `m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...)`. A test that injects a `TestLogger` and asserts on `InfoLogs` will see zero calls, because the log goes to a throwaway instance. The fake cannot be used to verify the middleware's output. It should return the receiver, or share the log state.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The ContextualLoggerMiddleware methods (QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, CollectMetrics) panic when a nil request is received. This occurs because they directly access req.PluginContext (via the instrumentContext function) without first checking if req is nil. This is a regression, as previous middleware layers gracefully handled nil requests.

The traceID is no longer logged for plugin requests. During a refactoring, the tracing import and the logic to extract and add traceID from the context to log parameters were removed from the LoggerMiddleware. The newly introduced ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add this information, resulting in missing traceID in plugin request logs and impacting debugging and request tracing capabilities.

false_positives.candidate:
New ContextualLoggerMiddleware and the reworked LoggerMiddleware have no tests

The PR moves the contextual-logger enrichment (endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID, uname) out of the metrics middleware into a new ContextualLoggerMiddleware. It also changes LoggerMiddleware to log through `m.logger.FromContext(ctx)` and drops the explicit pluginId, endpoint, uname, dsName, dsUID and traceID params. The only test change is renaming a constructor call in the metrics test. Nothing checks that the context ends up carrying the attributes, or that the 'Plugin Request Completed' log still contains the same fields. A regression in the middleware ordering or in `FromContext` would silently drop fields from the data-egress log.

Ordering requirement for the contextual logger middleware was dropped from the docs

The old InstrumentationMiddleware doc said it enriches the context with a contextual logger and therefore 'should live at the top of the middleware stack'. That responsibility now lives in ContextualLoggerMiddleware, but its doc comment has no ordering note. Its correctness still depends on running before LoggerMiddleware and any other downstream code that calls `logger.FromContext(ctx)`. A future reorder in `CreateMiddlewares` could silently drop the plugin and request fields from logs.

Stale 'instrumentation' naming left after the rename

The logger is still created as `log.New("plugin.instrumentation")`, so log output keeps the old 'instrumentation' name even though the middleware concept was renamed to metrics and contextual logger. In `metrics_middleware_test.go` the test function is still called `TestInstrumentationMiddleware`, and the local variable in `NewMetricsMiddleware` is still `imw`. This undercuts the stated goal of naming consistency. If the logger name is kept deliberately for log-query compatibility, say so.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Count-then-insert limit check is not atomic and can overshoot under concurrency

`CreateOrUpdateDevice` runs `CountDevices`, compares it with `deviceLimit`, and then does a separate upsert, with no transaction or lock. Concurrent first requests from many new devices, or from several Grafana instances in HA, can all see `count < limit` and all insert. The configured limit can then be exceeded by roughly the request concurrency. If the limit is meant to be hard, the check and insert need to be atomic (for example a conditional INSERT ... SELECT with the count in the same statement, or a transaction/lock). If it is meant to be soft, the docs should say so.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Rejected device is cached before the store call, so a retry bypasses the limit

`tagDeviceUI` calls `a.localCache.SetDefault(key, ...)` before `CreateOrUpdateDevice`. If the store returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, the key stays cached for 29 minutes. The next request from the same rejected device hits the cache at line 83, returns nil, and `Anonymous.Authenticate` lets the request through as an anonymous user. A rejected device is therefore blocked once and then allowed for the rest of the cache TTL, which defeats the feature. The cache key should only be set after a successful store call, or removed when the store returns an error.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
Device tagging is now synchronous on the request path and uses the request context

The previous fire-and-forget goroutine with its own 2-minute timeout context is replaced by a blocking `TagDevice(ctx, ...)` call. Every anonymous request that misses the local cache now waits on a COUNT query plus an upsert before authentication completes. If the request context is cancelled, the tagging fails. Synchronous behaviour is needed to enforce the limit, but it adds DB latency and a DB dependency to the auth path. Reviewers should be aware of this, and the tradeoff should be applied only when `AnonymousDeviceLimit > 0`.

Limit error is a plain error, so rejected users get an unhelpful generic auth failure

When the limit is hit, `Authenticate` returns the bare `anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached`, which is created with `fmt.Errorf` and carries no HTTP status or public message. The authn layer treats it as a generic authentication failure, so the user sees an opaque 401 or a redirect to login rather than a message that the anonymous device limit was reached. Using a typed error such as an `errutil` Unauthorized or Forbidden with a public message would give a deterministic status code and a useful message.

New `device_limit` option under [auth.anonymous] is undocumented

`auth.anonymous.device_limit` is read here, but `conf/defaults.ini`, `conf/sample.ini` and the configuration docs are not updated. Operators cannot discover the option, nor that 0 means unlimited. The PR description is also left as the unfilled template.

No test covers the limit-reached path through the service or client

The only new test is the store-level `TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit`. Nothing tests `AnonDeviceService.TagDevice` or `Anonymous.Authenticate` with a limit set. That means nothing exercises that the error propagates, that a rejected device is not cached, or that other tag errors are still only logged. A test of this kind would have caught the cache-before-store bug in `tagDeviceUI`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Debug logging at Error level, including the full ID list, on every batch

Each batch logs `r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", ..., "ids", ids, ...)` plus a second Error line after the delete. The same pattern is at lines 537, 554, 557, 576 and 579. Successful, routine cleanup therefore emits Error-level logs on every batch, on every run, even when zero rows are found. These lines dump the entire slice of IDs, which can be thousands of entries for large `AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize` values such as the 32767 used in the new test. This pollutes error monitoring and alerting and bloats log volume. The `"err", err` field is always nil at that point. Remove these lines or downgrade them to Debug without the full ID list.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup ticker interval changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute (unrelated to the fix)

`time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 10)` became `time.Minute * 1`. This is unrelated to the deadlock fix and looks like a leftover debugging change. Every cleanup job now runs 10x more often: snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, short URLs and query history. The annotation cleanup is the job that contends with inserts on MySQL, so more frequent runs raise the chance of hitting the deadlock this PR tries to avoid. The per-run timeout is 9 minutes, so a slow run can also overlap the next tick. Revert to 10 minutes.

false_positives.candidate:
Placeholder-based IN list breaks for large batch sizes on MySQL/Postgres

The old code deleted via a subquery with no bind parameters, so any `AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize` worked. The new code binds one `?` per ID, and only SQLite with batch size >999 gets the inline path. MySQL and Postgres have a hard limit of 65535 bind parameters per statement. A configured batch size above that now makes every cleanup fail with a 'too many placeholders' error, which is a regression for such configurations. The inline-literal fallback should also apply to other dialects, or the IDs should be chunked into sub-batches below the limit.

Quadratic string concatenation when inlining IDs for large SQLite batches

In the inline-ID branch, `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` re-copies the whole accumulated string for every ID. With a batch of 32767 IDs the string reaches about 250KB, so this performs gigabytes of copying and allocation per batch, and the test with 40003 rows runs it repeatedly. Use a `strings.Builder` (or `strings.Join` over formatted values) to make this linear.

Test case name no longer matches what it tests

The case 'running the max count delete again should not remove any annotations' relied on state left by the previous sub-test, so it really was a second run. The refactor now creates fresh data (9 annotations, 3 per type) and runs cleanup once. It only checks that nothing is deleted when the count is already at the limit, not idempotence of a repeated run. Rename it, or actually run the cleaner twice.

true_positives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete builds a contextual logger but stores the unenriched d.Log in the context

`log` is created with name, kind and method, but `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` stores the base logger. The downstream Storage and Legacy deletes therefore lose those values. true_positives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

In the async goroutine, the result of `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection` is recorded with `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ..., startLegacy)`. It should be `recordLegacyDuration`. The legacy latency and errors get mixed into the storage series, which already has an entry for this call, and the legacy metric never sees delete-collection.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.

Delete builds a contextual logger but stores the unenriched d.Log in the context

`log` is created with name, kind and method, but `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` stores the base logger. The downstream Storage and Legacy deletes therefore lose those values.
