Assuming `get_memory_info()` reports on the whole Redis cluster rather than only the buffer's assigned shards (not checked here), each call repeats the same `INFO` queries. `submit()` then does up to N times more Redis round trips per batch, and the used/available sums are inflated N-fold, which cancels out in the ratio. `max_processes or len(assigned_shards)` treats 0 as "one per shard", but a negative value from `--flusher-processes -1` (click `type=int` accepts it) is kept. `num_processes = min(-1, n)` is -1, so `process_to_shards_map` is empty and `i % self.num_processes` yields an index that is not in the map, which raises a KeyError at consumer startup. The restart path is where the `isinstance`/`kill` regression lives, and nothing exercises it.

The access token id therefore says `on...`, while only the offline session exists afterwards. CryptoProvider is a public SPI, and `int order()` is added as an abstract method. Any third-party or downstream implementation (custom FIPS/HSM providers and the like) no longer compiles. A binary that was compiled earlier throws AbstractMethodError inside CryptoIntegration.detectProvider when `CryptoProvider::order` is invoked, which fails startup. The old code threw IllegalStateException when more than one CryptoProvider was on the classpath. The new code sorts by order() and takes the first. If two of them are on the classpath, for example FIPS and default through a packaging mistake, the winner depends on the sort being stable over ServiceLoader order, which is classpath order. A FIPS deployment could silently run the non-FIPS BouncyCastle provider, where it used to fail fast. The ignored providers are reported only at debug level. All providers are also instantiated before the choice (the stream is collected eagerly), and the Default and FIPS constructors register global java.security providers as a side effect. AuthzClient.create now calls CryptoIntegration.init, so this class becomes the active provider whenever no higher-order provider is on the classpath. getSignature, getKeyFactory, getKeyPairGen, getAesCbcCipher, getAesGcmCipher, getSecretKeyFact, getX509CertFactory, getCertStore, getCertPathBuilder, createECParams, getPemUtils and getCertificateUtils all throw UnsupportedOperationException. `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()` uses the default curve (P-256), and that same key signs for ES256, ES384 and ES512. The assertion is only DER->RS->DER->RS, so a symmetric bug in the encoder and decoder would still pass. The test should use secp256r1, secp384r1 and secp521r1 for the corresponding algorithms. It should also compare against known vectors, or against another implementation, and cover small r/s values and values with the high bit set.

The right fix is to reject negative offsets, not to enable them.

`FixedQueuePool` is created once in `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` and passed to every `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` that `create_with_partitions` builds. Arroyo calls `close()`/`join()` on the current strategy on every partition revocation and then calls `create_with_partitions` again. `close()` and `join()` both call `queue_pool.shutdown()`, which sets `worker.shutdown = True`, calls `q.shutdown()` on every queue and joins the workers. After the first rebalance the replacement strategy is handed the same dead pool: the worker threads have exited and `queue.put` raises `ShutDown`. Combined with the broad `except` in `submit`, every later message is dropped and its offset is committed (see the next finding). The `OffsetTracker` is also shared across rebalances, so leftover offsets for revoked partitions can be committed later and rewind the group's progress. The pool needs to be owned by the factory and only shut down in `factory.shutdown()`, or be created per strategy instance, and the tracker should be reset for revoked partitions.

It is data loss when the failure is in `queue_pool.submit`, for example `queue.ShutDown` from a shut-down queue, or an error in `grouping_fn`. The message is never processed, its offset is committed past, and the only trace is a log line. Infrastructure failures should propagate, or the offset should not be completed, so the message is retried after a restart.

Queues are unbounded and poll() applies no backpressure, contrary to the class docstring

The strategy docstring promises "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but each queue is `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize`, and `poll()` only emits a gauge. `submit` never raises `MessageRejected`, so the consumer keeps pulling from Kafka at full speed. If one queue is slow or stuck, committed offsets stall at the first outstanding offset, which is exactly the case the PR describes. Meanwhile every later message is decoded and held in memory, each with both the decoded result and the original message in `WorkItem`. A stuck worker therefore leads to unbounded memory growth and a large reprocessing burst on restart. Use bounded queues and reject or pause submission when the target queue is full.

Commit logic treats any gap in offsets as unprocessed and stalls commits permanently

`get_committable_offsets` walks `range(start, max_offset + 1)` and stops at the first offset that is not in `all_offsets`. Kafka partitions can legitimately have non-contiguous offsets (transaction markers, compacted topics, retention). The tracker only knows offsets it was given, so it cannot tell "never delivered" from "in flight". After such a gap, `highest_committable` never advances. Commits stop for that partition, and `all_offsets` and `outstanding` grow without bound. The tests (`test_offset_gaps_block_commits`, `test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_gaps`) enshrine this behaviour. Commit decisions should rely on the lowest outstanding offset (commit everything below it), not on contiguity of submitted offsets.

Kafka commit is invoked from a background thread while the main thread polls

`_commit_loop` runs in its own daemon thread and calls `commit_function`, which wraps the arroyo `commit` callable. That callable is wired to the `StreamProcessor` and its Kafka consumer, which stages and commits offsets and are not thread-safe. They are normally used only from the processor's run loop, the same thread that polls and handles assignment and revocation callbacks. Calling them concurrently from the commit thread risks racing with `poll`, assignment and revocation state, and committing partitions that were just revoked. The strategy should hand the committable offsets back to the main thread (for example, compute them in `poll()` and call `commit` there) instead of committing from a separate thread.

`shutdown()` sets `worker.shutdown = True` before calling `q.shutdown(immediate=False)`. The worker loop checks `self.shutdown` at the top of each iteration, so each worker finishes only its current item and exits, leaving the rest of its queue unprocessed. `close()` also joins the commit thread before shutting down the pool, so work finished during shutdown is never committed. This does not lose offsets, because they simply stay uncommitted, but it contradicts the docstring and causes avoidable reprocessing. `test_stats_reporting` asserts `stats["total_items"] > 0` immediately after submitting, but three live workers may already have drained all 10 trivial items. `test_different_groups_distributed` (line 106) asserts that 20 string keys hit all 3 queues. Python's string hash is randomized per process, so there is a small chance (about 0.1%) that some queue is missed. Both tests should use deterministic setup, such as blocking the workers or choosing keys by computed queue index.

In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.

In the dashboard-widget split flow the function is called with `discover` and `(query) AND !event.type:transaction`, or with `scoped_dataset` for the transaction-like split. Its additional concern about the raw request query does not negate the match.

false_positives.candidate:
60s eligibility cache is stale, never invalidated, and runs before the cheap dataset check

The allowlist result is cached for 60s per (org, hash of project ids). `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is defined but never called, so removing a project from `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` keeps returning upsampled counts for up to a minute. `options.get` is already served from an in-process cache, so the extra cache round trip buys little. The cache lookup and write also happen before `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform`. Every stats request on transactions, spans or metrics therefore pays a cache get and set for a decision that can never be True. The key also uses `hash(tuple(...))` instead of the ids themselves, so two different project sets can collide and share a wrong cached result. Do the dataset check first, and either drop the cache or invalidate it from the option-change path with an explicit id-based key.

Substring match on raw request query misclassifies negated and mixed queries as error-only

`_is_error_focused_query` returns True if the lowercased `query` GET param contains the substring `event.type:error`. That also matches `!event.type:error`, `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction`, and any value that merely starts with `error`. Queries that exclude errors or include transactions are then upsampled. `sum(sample_weight)` is meaningless or zero for transactions, so those counts come out wrong. A proper parse of the search filters is needed instead of a substring test.

upsampled_count uses sum(sample_weight) with no fallback for missing weights

`toInt64(sum(sample_weight))` returns 0 or undercounts for any error row where `sample_weight` is NULL, 0 or absent. That includes events ingested before the column was populated and events from allowlisted projects whose SDK sends no client sample rate. The code comment says the column is assumed to exist for all events, but nothing enforces it. For those rows the chart count becomes lower than the real `count()`, so it is a silent regression. Use something like `sum(coalesce(sample_weight, 1))`, or keep `count()` when weights are missing.

upsampled_count is a public query function but references a column absent from non-error datasets

Unlike the neighbouring function marked `private=True`, `upsampled_count` is publicly selectable by users. It depends on the `sample_weight` column, which the transactions dataset does not have, as the PR's own helper docstring says. A user calling `upsampled_count()` against transactions through the shared discover config will get a Snuba error. It should be private, or restricted to the errors dataset.

RPC upsampling branches are dead code

`use_rpc` is only true for `spans_rpc` and `ourlogs`. `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` returns False for every dataset other than errors and discover. The `upsampling_enabled` branches in the RPC and RPC top-events paths can therefore never run. The `upsampled_count() as count` string is also not a valid RPC y-axis. The branches add misleading code and should be removed.

Docstrings and comments contradict the actual caching behaviour

`_are_all_projects_error_upsampled` says it reads the allowlist fresh each time to always have the latest configuration. Its only caller caches the result for 60s, so the statement is false. The endpoint comments ("This cached result ensures consistent behavior", "most current schema assumptions", "better query optimization and caching") describe nothing the code does and mislead maintainers.

Whitespace-only lines with trailing spaces were added in the endpoint (around lines 223, 234, 278) and throughout `error_upsampling.py` docstrings and blank lines. This will fail the repo's formatting and lint hooks (black, flake8 W291/W293).

Core eligibility function, cache behaviour and edge cases are untested

`is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` is not unit-tested, including its cache hit, miss and invalidation paths. Nothing covers `!event.type:error` or mixed queries, the top_events path, or the dashboard-split path. `self.snuba_params` is built in `setUp` but never used. The endpoint tests rely on freshly created project ids to avoid cache pollution rather than clearing the cache.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Underscore-joined denial key is ambiguous and can deny the wrong resource

The key joins userUID, action, name and parent with `_`, and these values can contain underscores. `(name="a_b", parent="c")` and `(name="a", parent="b_c")` both produce `..._a_b_c`. A cached denial for one resource then wrongly denies the other for up to 30s. The key also starts with the same `perm_<uid>_<action>` prefix as `userPermCacheKey`, which makes cross-key clashes possible if values contain underscores. Use an unambiguous separator or encoding, or a distinct prefix such as `perm_denied_`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify ambiguous underscore-concatenated denial cache keys that can collide when components contain underscores, causing incorrect cached permission denials. The candidate provides a concrete example of the same underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache key omits identity type, so renderer and anonymous share denials

`userPermDenialCacheKey` is built from `checkReq.UserUID` (the raw subject ID), not the identity type. `anonymous:0` and `render:0` both yield UserUID `0` (the tests use exactly these subjects). If an anonymous check on dashboard X is denied, the key `<ns>.perm_0_dashboards:read_X_<folder>` is stored. A `render:0` check on the same dashboard within 30s then hits that entry in `Check` and is denied. The renderer holds a wildcard read grant, so image rendering can fail spuriously. Include the identity type in the key.

Every non-allowed check not already in the denial cache hits the permission DB

Cached permissions that do not allow the request now fall through to `getIdentityPermissions`. `getUserPermissions` no longer consults `permCache`, so it always runs the permission query, and the denial cache is keyed per (name, folder). A user or client probing many distinct resources the user cannot access triggers one full permission query per resource. Singleflight only dedups concurrent calls for the same user and action. The first denied check for each resource therefore costs a DB round trip, which amplifies load. Consider rate-limiting the refetch, for example a short per-user/action refresh cooldown, instead of re-querying on every miss.

Requery path still uses a stale cached folder tree, then caches the resulting denial

After a cache miss, permissions are re-fetched from the DB, but `checkPermission` → `checkInheritedPermissions` → `buildFolderTree` still reads the folder tree from `folderCache` (30s TTL). Suppose a user with inherited access via parent folder P creates subfolder C and a dashboard in C. If the cached tree predates C, `tree.Ancestors(C)` is empty, so the check returns denied. This PR then writes a 30s denial entry for it. The newly created nested folder or dashboard stays inaccessible for up to 30s, which is the scenario the PR is meant to fix. The folder tree should be refreshed on the requery path, or denials caused by a possibly stale tree should not be cached.

Denial entries are never invalidated and can mask a permission granted shortly after

A denial is cached for 30s with no invalidation. It is checked before the cached permissions and before the DB requery. If a check for a resource runs before its permission rows exist, or before a grant takes effect, the user is denied for the full TTL even though the DB now allows it. For example, a check may run between resource creation and permission assignment. That is the same "cannot fetch what I just created" symptom the PR targets. Consider a much shorter TTL for denials, or invalidation on resource creation or permission change.

Tests do not cover writing the denial entry, and a dead cacheHit branch remains

`TestService_CacheCheck` only checks that a pre-seeded denial entry is honored. No test verifies that a real denied `Check` writes `permDenialCache`, that a repeated denied check skips the DB (via `store.calls`), or that anonymous and renderer identities are handled. List fallback to the DB on a cache miss is untested. Separately, removing the "cached" case from `TestService_getUserPermissions` leaves the `cacheHit` field and its assertions as dead code, because no case sets `cacheHit: true`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

true_positives.golden_comment: OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OAuth `state` is a deterministic pipeline signature, not a per-session nonce

The `state` sent to GitHub and later compared (line 412) is `pipeline.signature`. It is derived from the pipeline's views and is the same for every user and org; the tests reuse the same hard-coded value for two different orgs and users. It is therefore guessable and gives no CSRF or session binding for the OAuth authorize round trip. Anyone can craft a callback URL with their own `code` and the known `state`. The comparison is also a plain `!=` rather than a constant-time compare. For a security fix whose description lists the state check as a protection, use a random, session-bound value.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same issue: OAuth state uses the static, deterministic pipeline.signature instead of a random value generated for each request. The candidate's additional security observations do not change this match.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
KeyError/500 when existing Integration has no `sender` metadata

`integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` assumes `sender` is always present. `build_integration` only stores it when `state.get("sender")` is truthy, so integrations created through the pipeline flow without a prior webhook, or created before sender tracking, have no `sender`. For such an Integration that has no OrganizationIntegration (for example, a re-install after the org integration was removed), the lookup raises KeyError and the user gets a 500 instead of the friendly error page. Use `.get` and treat missing data as a validation failure or handle it explicitly.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify an unchecked access to integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] that raises KeyError when sender metadata was not set during integration creation.

false_positives.candidate:
GitHub user check is skipped whenever no Integration row exists yet

The authenticated-user comparison (lines 500-505) only runs after `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id)` succeeds. The `except Integration.DoesNotExist` branch at 481-482 returns `pipeline.next_step()` without comparing `github_authenticated_user` to anyone. `installation_id` comes from the query string and takes precedence over the bound state (line 448). If the installation webhook has not been processed yet (the user is redirected at the same time the webhook fires) or was never delivered, anyone who supplies that installation_id gets it linked to their org. `build_integration` then fetches the installation with the app JWT. `test_basic_flow` exercises exactly this path with no webhook, so the PR's stated guarantee that the pipeline fails on a user mismatch does not hold. A failed or late webhook should be treated as a failure or verified some other way, not as success.

Network/HTTP failures in the token exchange and user lookup are not handled

`safe_urlopen(...)` at line 423 is outside the `try`, so connection errors or timeouts raise and produce a 500. `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` at line 434 also performs an HTTP request and can raise on non-2xx responses or network errors; only the missing-`login` case is handled. These GitHub-side failures should yield the same friendly `error(...)` response as the other failure modes the PR describes.

Authorize URL query string is built by string interpolation without encoding

`client_id`, `state` and `redirect_uri` are interpolated directly into the authorize URL. `redirect_uri` is a full URL containing `:` and `/`, and it is not percent-encoded. It works with GitHub today, but it is fragile, for example with a customized `url-prefix`, and `urlencode` should be used.

test_installation_not_found no longer tests the installation-not-found path

The test still stubs the installation lookup with a 404. It now sends a bogus `state` (`ddd023d8...`), so the flow ends in the state-mismatch error and asserts the generic "Invalid installation request." message. The `IntegrationError("The GitHub installation could not be found.")` branch in `build_integration` is therefore no longer covered, and the old assertion was silently replaced. The test now passes for a reason unrelated to its name.

Only one of the new failure modes (and no success case for an existing Integration) is tested

The PR lists three failure causes: user mismatch, state mismatch, and a failed `code` exchange. Only the user mismatch is tested. Nothing covers a wrong `state`, an `access_token` exchange failure, a `/user` response with no `login`, or an Integration that exists with no `sender` metadata. There is also no positive test where the authenticated GitHub user matches `metadata["sender"]["login"]` for a pre-existing Integration. Without these, the new validation can regress, or crash as in the KeyError case, unnoticed.

false_positives.candidate:
Invalidation-on-update decision uses the org-aware wrapped model as the 'original'

`update()` takes `idpById = getById(...)`, which returns the anonymous org-aware wrapper. Its `isEnabled()` also depends on whether the organization and the organization feature are enabled. `registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate` evaluates `getLoginPredicate()` on this wrapper, so `test(original)` can be false even though the IDP is stored as enabled and is present in the cached login list (the cache is filled from the DB, where only the IDP's own `enabled` counts). Example: the org is disabled, the IDP is stored enabled, and an admin sets it to disabled. Both `test(original)` and `test(updated)` are false, so the early return skips invalidation. The cached login list still holds the now-disabled IDP, and callers other than the login bean (which re-checks `isEnabled`) see a stale entry. Evaluate the predicate on the raw stored model (for example `idpDelegate.getById`), or always invalidate when the org-aware wrapper is involved.

Per-organization search keys bloat and thrash a single cache entry per fetch mode

All searches for a fetch mode share one `IdentityProviderListQuery` entry, and `searchKey` is the organizationId. For `REALM_ONLY` the delegate ignores organizationId, so the same result is stored once per org. For `ALL`, every organization's set repeats all realm-level login IDPs. Each first lookup for a new org takes the `cached == null` branch, which calls `cache.invalidateObject(cacheKey)` and rebuilds a new query by copying all previous searches. In a realm with many organizations this means O(orgs) growth of one entry, O(n²) copying, and repeated local invalidation/re-adds on the hot login path. Normalise the key (use `""` for `REALM_ONLY`) and/or key the entry by organization instead of piling everything into one query.

remove() now always hits the DB even when the IDP is in the cache

`storedIdp = idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias)` runs unconditionally. Before, the DB lookup only happened when the alias key was already invalidated in this transaction; otherwise the cached entry was used. The result is only needed to evaluate the login predicate, so every removal now pays an extra query. Reuse the cached model (`cached.getIdentityProvider()`) when available, and only fall back to the delegate when the entry is missing or invalid.

Test checks only cache presence, never the returned results or invalidation on creating/removing an eligible IDP

`testCacheIDPForLogin` inspects the `IdentityProviderListQuery` contents but never asserts what `getForLogin` actually returns on a cache hit (including the wrapped, org-aware models and the HashSet reassembly). It only covers creating a non-eligible IDP and removing a non-eligible IDP, so the branches that matter are untested. These are: creating an eligible IDP, removing an eligible IDP (`registerIDPLoginInvalidation` in `create`/`remove`), disabling an eligible IDP, and organization disable/enable. A regression in those invalidation paths would go unnoticed.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:

`enabled := !IsEnabledGlobally(FlagSqlExpressions)` followed by `if enabled { return false }; return false` returns false on every path. The inverted `!` and the identical branches will confuse the next maintainer and invite a mistaken 'fix' that re-enables the path. The call also dereferences `h.features`, which the SQL branch did not do before, so a reader built with nil features would now panic on any SQL query. A user who enables the `sqlExpressions` feature toggle gets `sqlExpressions is not implemented` for any SQL expression. The toggle's registry description and docs still say it enables SQL expressions, and the frontend can still offer the option. The behavior (deliberately disabled for a security fix) and the user-facing message are inconsistent. The flag's description or docs should be updated to say it is disabled, or the message should say SQL expressions are disabled.

No tests added or updated for the disabled SQL expression behavior

The PR touches no test files. `sql.TablesList` and `NewSQLCommand` now always fail because the stub `RunCommands` returns 'not implemented'. Any existing test that expects a successful `TablesList` or `NewSQLCommand` (for example `parser_test.go` or `sql_command_test.go`) will fail or must be removed, and none are updated here. Legacy UnmarshalSQLCommand path gives a generic, misleading error

The `UnmarshalSQLCommand` -> `NewSQLCommand` path has no explicit check for SQL being disabled. It fails closed only because the stub `RunCommands` errors inside `TablesList`. The caller then sees `error reading SQL command` (a bad-request about invalid SQL), and the real reason is only in server logs at Warn/Error level. true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
No re-check of the cache after taking the write lock

The cache is read under RLock, the lock is released, and the write Lock is taken afterwards without checking the cache again. On a cold start in non-dev mode, N concurrent requests all see nil. They then queue on Lock(), and each one in turn reads and parses assets-manifest.json and re-applies the CDN URL, even though the first one already filled the cache. The result is correct but the work is redundant, and every request waits behind that serialized I/O. Re-checking `entryPointAssetsCache != nil && cfg.Env != setting.Dev` right after acquiring the write lock avoids this.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the missing cache re-check after acquiring the write lock, which allows concurrent goroutines to redundantly populate an already-filled cache.

false_positives.candidate:
No regression test for the race being fixed

The PR fixes a data race but adds no test. A test that calls GetWebAssets from several goroutines and is run with `-race` would show the race is gone and keep it from coming back. It could also check that the cache is populated once in non-dev mode.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.

Debug logging at Error level, including the full ID list, on every batch

false_positives.candidate:
Quadratic string concatenation when inlining IDs for large SQLite batches

In the inline-ID branch, `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` re-copies the whole accumulated string for every ID. With a batch of 32767 IDs the string reaches about 250KB, so this performs gigabytes of copying and allocation per batch, and the test with 40003 rows runs it repeatedly. Use a `strings.Builder` (or `strings.Join` over formatted values) to make this linear.

The old code deleted via a subquery with no bind parameters, so any `AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize` worked. The new code binds one `?` per ID, and only SQLite with batch size >999 gets the inline path. MySQL and Postgres have a hard limit of 65535 bind parameters per statement. A configured batch size above that now makes every cleanup fail with a 'too many placeholders' error, which is a regression for such configurations. The inline-literal fallback should also apply to other dialects, or the IDs should be chunked into sub-batches below the limit.

Test case name no longer matches what it tests

The case 'running the max count delete again should not remove any annotations' relied on state left by the previous sub-test, so it really was a second run. The refactor now creates fresh data (9 annotations, 3 per type) and runs cleanup once. It only checks that nothing is deleted when the count is already at the limit, not idempotence of a repeated run. Rename it, or actually run the cleaner twice.

That context is cancelled as soon as the HTTP request finishes, and Create/Update/Delete return right after spawning the goroutine. The legacy call then runs with an already-cancelled or soon-cancelled context. SQL-backed legacy storage will usually fail with `context canceled`, so the 'safe measure' legacy write silently does not happen. Detach cancellation with `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` (or a fresh context carrying the needed values) before applying the 10s timeout. The unit tests use `context.Background()`, so they cannot catch this.

Storage create failure is recorded as a legacy duration

When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)`. The failure came from Storage, so it should call `recordStorageDuration`. As written, unified-storage failures are counted under the legacy metric, and the storage error metric for create is never incremented. The same mistake is in Update at line 129.

Storage update failure is recorded as a legacy duration

On `d.Storage.Update` error the code calls `recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` instead of `recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`. Storage update errors are therefore attributed to the legacy backend and storage metrics undercount failures.

Legacy DeleteCollection duration is recorded with the storage metric

In the async goroutine, the result of `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection` is recorded with `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ..., startLegacy)`. It should be `recordLegacyDuration`. The legacy latency and errors get mixed into the storage series, which already has an entry for this call, and the legacy metric never sees delete-collection.

The previous implementation wrapped the storage result in `updateWrapper` so legacy received the exact object that was persisted. Now the raw `objInfo` is passed to `Legacy.Update` in a goroutine. For patch/apply requests, `UpdatedObject` is recomputed against the legacy store's own copy. That copy can differ from unified storage, including its resourceVersion, which risks conflicts or divergent data. The same `objInfo` is also used concurrently with the request handler after the function returns.

Errors from async legacy writes are neither logged nor surfaced

The old code logged legacy failures with the object context. In the new goroutines (Create 55-56, Update 139-140, Delete 112-113, DeleteCollection 165-166) the error is only turned into a boolean for a metric and then discarded. When legacy diverges from unified storage there is no log line saying which object or why, which makes the 'safe measure' write effectively unobservable. Log the error with the name/kind logger in each goroutine.

Tests never verify the async legacy write, which is the core of mode 3

None of the Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection tests assert that the legacy store is called after a successful storage write (for example `assert.Eventually` plus `m.AssertCalled`). They also do not assert that it is not called when storage fails. The legacy goroutines run unsynchronized and may outlive the test. The mock is shared between the legacy and storage stores, so the 'legacy' mock setups are satisfied by whichever side calls first. All tests use `context.Background()`, so the request-context cancellation problem cannot be detected. The tests would pass even if the legacy write were removed.

These look like accidental output from a local `go work sync` and add noise to a PR about dual-writer mode 3.

false_positives.candidate:
Working-hours check rejects any slot that falls outside any one range for that day

`workingHours.find(cb)` returns true, and the slot is rejected, as soon as the slot lies outside any single working-hour entry whose `days` includes the slot's weekday. A user with split availability on the same days (for example 09:00–12:00 and 13:00–17:00, or a lunch break) has two entries for those days. A slot inside the first range is always outside the second, so `find` matches and `checkIfIsAvailable` returns false. Every slot for such a host is then dropped. The check should pass if the slot lies inside at least one range (`!workingHours.some(contains slot)`), and it should apply only when entries exist for that day. Because `...schedule` is spread into every fixed and loose host check, this regresses ordinary non-round-robin events too.

The `dateOverrides.find` callback returns true (slot unavailable) as soon as the slot is outside any single override on that date. A host with two override ranges on one day (for example 09:00–12:00 and 14:00–17:00) has each valid slot fail the other range's checks. A 10:00 slot is before the 14:00 range and so returns true, and the function returns false. The slot has to be rejected only if it fits none of the overrides for that date. Cal.com's date-override UI allows multiple ranges per date, so this makes valid slots disappear for those hosts.

After shifting the override start to real UTC, the code matches an override to a slot only if the UTC date of the override start equals the UTC date of the slot start. An override that spans UTC midnight is common for hosts far from UTC, for example 06:00–12:00 in Sydney, which runs from 20:00Z the previous day to 02:00Z. Slots on the later UTC date never match, so `dateOverrideExist` stays false. Those slots fall through to the regular working-hours check and the override is ignored for them. The comparison should use the organizer-local date, or check whether the slot falls inside the [start, end) instant range.

`activeOverrides` still selects overrides whose raw `start` (the organizer's wall-clock time encoded as UTC) falls between the invitee's start and end of day. The new code then shifts the minutes by the invitee-vs-organizer offset. The day selection and the time conversion therefore use different frames. For an invitee far ahead of the organizer (for example UTC+10 and an organizer in IST), the override's real instant is on invitee day D, but the raw start falls on D+1. The override is dropped from day D and applied to D+1 at the shifted time. The filter should run on the converted start, using the same offset.

Shifted override minutes wrap at midnight, producing inverted or wrongly-placed ranges

Start and end are converted to `hour()*60 + minute()` after adding the offset, which discards the day. If the shift pushes an override across the invitee's midnight, start and end wrap to small values. A late-evening override such as 18:00–23:59 in the organizer's timezone, viewed from a timezone further east, can give an end value smaller than the start, which `buildSlots` skips (`start >= end`), so the slots vanish. If only one side wraps, the range is placed on the wrong day. Clamp or split the range at the invitee's day boundaries instead of taking time-of-day modulo 24h.

`dayjs(override.start.toString())` re-parses a host-locale string such as 'Tue Jul 04 2023 14:00:00 GMT+0000 (...)'. That is implementation-dependent and drops milliseconds; pass `override.start` directly. `override.timeZone` is optional in the updated `TimeRange` type. When it is missing, `.tz(undefined)` silently falls back to the runtime's local timezone, giving a different offset on client and server.

The PR's main fix is that fixed hosts' date overrides and working hours are enforced in `checkIfIsAvailable` for round-robin events. The only new test is a personal-event invitee-timezone case. Nothing covers a ROUND_ROBIN event with a fixed host having an override, multiple overrides on one day, split working hours, or an override spanning UTC midnight. Those are the cases where the bugs above show up. Also, `toHaveTimeSlots` only iterates the actual slots, so a result with fewer slots than expected still passes.

true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative cursor offsets are passed straight into queryset slicing, based on a false claim about the ORM

The comment says the ORM "properly handles negative slicing automatically". It does not: Django querysets raise `ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported` for a negative start or stop. Cursor offsets come from the user-supplied `cursor` query param (`Cursor.from_string` accepts any `int` for the offset, including negatives, with no validation). A request with `optimized_pagination=true` and a cursor like `0:-5:0` therefore reaches `queryset[start_offset:stop]` and returns a 500. The comments ("access to data beyond normal pagination bounds", "safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level") suggest the intent is to bypass pagination bounds. If negative indexing did work, it would let a caller read from the end of the dataset and sidestep the offset checks that other paginators enforce with `BadPaginationError`. The right fix is to reject negative offsets, not to enable them.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: OptimizedCursorPaginator passes negative cursor offsets into Django queryset slicing, which does not support negative indexing and raises an error (500). The exception type differs (AssertionError vs ValueError), but the underlying issue is the same.

organization_context.member can be None, causing AttributeError

`enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` dereferences `member` without a None check. For callers authenticated without an org membership (for example an API token or key with `org:write`, or a non-member user), `member` is `None`. true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removing the BuildIndex lock allows duplicate concurrent builds, and the overwritten index is never closed

The old whole-function lock serialized builds, and it also made `GetIndex` (which takes `RLock`) block until a build finished. With the lock removed, `GetIndex` returns nil while a build is in flight. Two concurrent callers of `getOrCreateIndex` for the same key (for example two searches, or a search plus a watch event, for a resource under `InitMinCount`) then both run a full `BuildIndex`. The work is duplicated and `IndexTenants` is incremented twice. For file-backed indexes the second `bleve.New(dir)` fails on the existing directory. For in-memory indexes the second build silently replaces the first in `b.cache` without closing it, which leaks the old bleve index. `BuildIndex` needs per-key de-duplication (singleflight or a per-key lock), or at least a re-check and close of any existing cache entry when inserting.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same race caused by narrowing the BuildIndex lock: concurrent goroutines can build the same key's index, with the candidate additionally noting the leaked overwritten index.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.

TotalDocs iterates the cache map without cacheMu, and this PR adds a startup caller

`TotalDocs` ranges over `b.cache` without taking `cacheMu`, while `BuildIndex` writes to the same map under `cacheMu.Lock()`. The PR now calls `s.search.TotalDocs()` from `searchSupport.init` for the new log line. That call runs right after the goroutine consuming `WatchWriteEvents` is started, and that goroutine calls `handleEvent`, then `getOrCreateIndex`, then `BuildIndex`, which writes to the map. The first event for a resource that was skipped by `InitMinCount` therefore races with the unlocked read. Go can abort the process with 'fatal error: concurrent map iteration and map write'. `TotalDocs` should take `cacheMu.RLock()`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same race: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization while the newly started event watcher can concurrently trigger BuildIndex map writes, risking a concurrent map read/write panic.

Stop() sets initErr but nothing reads it any more, so requests are no longer rejected during shutdown

Every handler used to call `s.Init(ctx)`, which returned `s.initErr`. `Stop` set `initErr` to 'service is stopping' or 'service is stopped', so requests arriving during or after shutdown failed fast. This PR removes all of those calls and `Init` is now only called from the constructor. `Stop` still writes `initErr`, but nothing consumes it. A cheap stopped-state check should be restored in the handlers, or the dead state removed.

false_positives.candidate:
Strategy close() shuts down the factory-shared queue pool, which is reused after the first rebalance

`FixedQueuePool` is created once in `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` and passed to every `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` that `create_with_partitions` builds. Arroyo calls `close()`/`join()` on the current strategy on every partition revocation and then calls `create_with_partitions` again. `close()` and `join()` both call `queue_pool.shutdown()`, which sets `worker.shutdown = True`, calls `q.shutdown()` on every queue and joins the workers. After the first rebalance the replacement strategy is handed the same dead pool: the worker threads have exited and `queue.put` raises `ShutDown`. Combined with the broad `except` in `submit`, every later message is dropped and its offset is committed (see the next finding). The `OffsetTracker` is also shared across rebalances, so leftover offsets for revoked partitions can be committed later and rewind the group's progress. The pool needs to be owned by the factory and only shut down in `factory.shutdown()`, or be created per strategy instance, and the tracker should be reset for revoked partitions.

Any exception in submit() marks the offset completed, so failed enqueues are silently dropped and committed

The `except Exception` branch in `submit` calls `add_offset` and `complete_offset` for the message, which makes it immediately committable. That is fine for an undecodable payload. It is data loss when the failure is in `queue_pool.submit`, for example `queue.ShutDown` from a shut-down queue, or an error in `grouping_fn`. The message is never processed, its offset is committed past, and the only trace is a log line. Infrastructure failures should propagate, or the offset should not be completed, so the message is retried after a restart.

Queues are unbounded and poll() applies no backpressure, contrary to the class docstring

The strategy docstring promises "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but each queue is `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize`, and `poll()` only emits a gauge. `submit` never raises `MessageRejected`, so the consumer keeps pulling from Kafka at full speed. If one queue is slow or stuck, committed offsets stall at the first outstanding offset, which is exactly the case the PR describes. Meanwhile every later message is decoded and held in memory, each with both the decoded result and the original message in `WorkItem`. A stuck worker therefore leads to unbounded memory growth and a large reprocessing burst on restart. Use bounded queues and reject or pause submission when the target queue is full.

Commit logic treats any gap in offsets as unprocessed and stalls commits permanently

`get_committable_offsets` walks `range(start, max_offset + 1)` and stops at the first offset that is not in `all_offsets`. Kafka partitions can legitimately have non-contiguous offsets (transaction markers, compacted topics, retention). The tracker only knows offsets it was given, so it cannot tell "never delivered" from "in flight". After such a gap, `highest_committable` never advances. Commits stop for that partition, and `all_offsets` and `outstanding` grow without bound. The tests (`test_offset_gaps_block_commits`, `test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_gaps`) enshrine this behaviour. Commit decisions should rely on the lowest outstanding offset (commit everything below it), not on contiguity of submitted offsets.

Kafka commit is invoked from a background thread while the main thread polls

`_commit_loop` runs in its own daemon thread and calls `commit_function`, which wraps the arroyo `commit` callable. That callable is wired to the `StreamProcessor` and its Kafka consumer, which stages and commits offsets and are not thread-safe. They are normally used only from the processor's run loop, the same thread that polls and handles assignment and revocation callbacks. Calling them concurrently from the commit thread risks racing with `poll`, assignment and revocation state, and committing partitions that were just revoked. The strategy should hand the committable offsets back to the main thread (for example, compute them in `poll()` and call `commit` there) instead of committing from a separate thread.

"Graceful" shutdown discards items still queued

`shutdown()` sets `worker.shutdown = True` before calling `q.shutdown(immediate=False)`. The worker loop checks `self.shutdown` at the top of each iteration, so each worker finishes only its current item and exits, leaving the rest of its queue unprocessed. `close()` also joins the commit thread before shutting down the pool, so work finished during shutdown is never committed. This does not lose offsets, because they simply stay uncommitted, but it contradicts the docstring and causes avoidable reprocessing. Either drain the queues (let `queue.ShutDown` end the workers) or fix the docstring.

Probabilistic assertions in queue tests can flake

`test_stats_reporting` asserts `stats["total_items"] > 0` immediately after submitting, but three live workers may already have drained all 10 trivial items. `test_different_groups_distributed` (line 106) asserts that 20 string keys hit all 3 queues. Python's string hash is randomized per process, so there is a small chance (about 0.1%) that some queue is missed. Both tests should use deterministic setup, such as blocking the workers or choosing keys by computed queue index.

The script evicts down to a hard-coded 1000 members with `zpopmin`. `SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans` still defaults to 1001 and is no longer used anywhere, because the Python-side check in `_load_segment_data` was removed. The configured limit and the real limit now disagree and the parameter is dead. Previously an oversized segment logged an error and emitted `segment_span_count_exceeded`. Now spans are dropped silently, with no metric or log for how many were evicted. Pass the limit into the script as an ARGV value from `max_segment_spans`, and have the script or caller emit a metric when it evicts.

Scores are now span end timestamps, and eviction relies on `zpopmin` removing the oldest. `zunionstore` defaults to `AGGREGATE SUM`. If the same payload is present in both sets being merged, for example after a Kafka redelivery, its score is added to itself and becomes roughly 2×timestamp. That span is then treated as the newest and survives eviction ahead of genuinely newer spans. Use `AGGREGATE MAX` (or `MIN`). The same applies to the second union on line 53.

The PR is titled 'eviction during insert', but the tests only add `end_timestamp_precise` to existing fixtures. In `PollFeed` this aborts the whole `rss.items.each` loop, so one deleted topic blocks all later imports every hour. Guard against a nil post, and either skip it or recreate the topic.

The `-c/--category` option and its lookup are removed, and `PostCreator` is replaced by `TopicEmbed.import_remote`. All imported topics now land in the default category, and `created_at: Date.parse(t[:created_at])` is dropped, so topics get today's date instead of the Disqus thread date. The importer now also does a live HTTP fetch of every thread link via `open(url).read`, with no error handling. A single 404 or timeout raises and aborts the whole import. None of this is mentioned in the PR.

This PR rewrites an already-existing migration (`create_top_topics`) to use `force: true`, which drops and recreates `top_topics` if the migration is ever re-run. That is unrelated to embedding and destructive. `create_topic_embeds` also uses `force: true` (line 3) and would drop an existing `topic_embeds` table and its data. Editing historical migrations, and the whitespace-only change to `migrate_word_counts`, should be left out of this PR.

`ruby-readability` and `simple-rss` are added to the shared Gemfile, but only `Gemfile_rails4.lock` is updated. The repo is dual-booted, and `Gemfile.lock` (RAILS3=1 mode) is not touched. Bundler in that mode will have to re-resolve, or fail with a frozen or deployment lockfile, and CI for the Rails 3 boot is likely to break.

With precompiled assets in production the stylesheet raises or 404s, so the embed iframe renders unstyled or errors. `embed.js` will not be served either.

Each unknown embed URL can trigger a full synchronous feed poll

`perform_retrieve` calls `Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({})` inline whenever an unknown embed URL is requested. The throttle key is per URL, so requests for many different URLs each fetch and parse the entire feed and import every item in a Sidekiq worker, with no timeout. Since the `embed/best` endpoint enqueues this job for any unseen URL, it is an easy amplification path. Throttle at the feed level (e.g. one key for the feed URL) rather than per embed URL.

With no stubs, `embeddable_host` is blank, so the request fails in `ensure_embeddable` before `params.require(:embed_url)` is ever reached, and the failure is an InvalidAccess response, not a 404. The missing-parameter path is never exercised. There is also no test for a referer whose host differs from `embeddable_host`. The new `PollFeed#poll_feed`, `TopicEmbed.import_remote` and the update branch of `import` also have no meaningful coverage.

As written, `end > workingHour.endTime` is just a check on the start time, so a slot that starts inside working hours but runs past their end passes. The check is effectively broken.

`dayjs(date.start).add(...) === dayjs(date.end).add(...)` compares two freshly created objects by reference, so it never evaluates to true. This branch was meant to handle a zero-length override (the day marked unavailable). It is dead code, so that case relies on the later `isBefore`/`isAfter` checks. true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: === compares dayjs object references and is always false for freshly created objects. The candidate correctly recommends .isSame() (or .valueOf()) as the fix.

false_positives.candidate:
Working-hours check rejects any slot that falls outside any one range for that day

`workingHours.find(cb)` returns true, and the slot is rejected, as soon as the slot lies outside any single working-hour entry whose `days` includes the slot's weekday. A user with split availability on the same days (for example 09:00–12:00 and 13:00–17:00, or a lunch break) has two entries for those days. A slot inside the first range is always outside the second, so `find` matches and `checkIfIsAvailable` returns false. Every slot for such a host is then dropped. The check should pass if the slot lies inside at least one range (`!workingHours.some(contains slot)`), and it should apply only when entries exist for that day. Because `...schedule` is spread into every fixed and loose host check, this regresses ordinary non-round-robin events too.

Multiple date-override ranges on the same day make every slot unavailable

The `dateOverrides.find` callback returns true (slot unavailable) as soon as the slot is outside any single override on that date. A host with two override ranges on one day (for example 09:00–12:00 and 14:00–17:00) has each valid slot fail the other range's checks. A 10:00 slot is before the 14:00 range and so returns true, and the function returns false. The slot has to be rejected only if it fits none of the overrides for that date. Cal.com's date-override UI allows multiple ranges per date, so this makes valid slots disappear for those hosts.

Override matched by UTC calendar date of its start only; overrides crossing UTC midnight are skipped

After shifting the override start to real UTC, the code matches an override to a slot only if the UTC date of the override start equals the UTC date of the slot start. An override that spans UTC midnight is common for hosts far from UTC, for example 06:00–12:00 in Sydney, which runs from 20:00Z the previous day to 02:00Z. Slots on the later UTC date never match, so `dateOverrideExist` stays false. Those slots fall through to the regular working-hours check and the override is ignored for them. The comparison should use the organizer-local date, or check whether the slot falls inside the [start, end) instant range.

Override-to-day filter is not timezone-adjusted, but the time conversion now is

`activeOverrides` still selects overrides whose raw `start` (the organizer's wall-clock time encoded as UTC) falls between the invitee's start and end of day. The new code then shifts the minutes by the invitee-vs-organizer offset. The day selection and the time conversion therefore use different frames. For an invitee far ahead of the organizer (for example UTC+10 and an organizer in IST), the override's real instant is on invitee day D, but the raw start falls on D+1. The override is dropped from day D and applied to D+1 at the shifted time. The filter should run on the converted start, using the same offset.

Shifted override minutes wrap at midnight, producing inverted or wrongly-placed ranges

Start and end are converted to `hour()*60 + minute()` after adding the offset, which discards the day. If the shift pushes an override across the invitee's midnight, start and end wrap to small values. A late-evening override such as 18:00–23:59 in the organizer's timezone, viewed from a timezone further east, can give an end value smaller than the start, which `buildSlots` skips (`start >= end`), so the slots vanish. If only one side wraps, the range is placed on the wrong day. Clamp or split the range at the invitee's day boundaries instead of taking time-of-day modulo 24h.

`dayjs(override.start.toString())` re-parses a host-locale string such as 'Tue Jul 04 2023 14:00:00 GMT+0000 (...)'. That is implementation-dependent and drops milliseconds; pass `override.start` directly. `override.timeZone` is optional in the updated `TimeRange` type. When it is missing, `.tz(undefined)` silently falls back to the runtime's local timezone, giving a different offset on client and server.

The PR's main fix is that fixed hosts' date overrides and working hours are enforced in `checkIfIsAvailable` for round-robin events. The only new test is a personal-event invitee-timezone case. Nothing covers a ROUND_ROBIN event with a fixed host having an override, multiple overrides on one day, split working hours, or an override spanning UTC midnight. Those are the cases where the bugs above show up. Also, `toHaveTimeSlots` only iterates the actual slots, so a result with fewer slots than expected still passes.
